bases.narrative: My mother can't live on her own any more. My brother Daniel and I are making this decision, just the two of us; Mom has said she will go along with whatever we agree. Her doctor says either option is safe for her: Maple Court, an assisted-living home, or staying in her house with a daytime aide from the Brightside agency. Maple Court charges $6,200 a month, and her long-term-care policy pays $1,500 a month toward a facility but nothing toward home care. Brightside's quote for the aide is a flat $5,200 a month. Maple Court is 6 minutes from my apartment; Mom's house is 35 minutes away. Our rule: we will move Mom into Maple Court if and only if Maple Court's monthly charge minus what her policy pays is lower than Brightside's monthly fee; otherwise we will hire the aide. Nothing else is part of this decision for Daniel and me.
bases.question: Should we move Mom into Maple Court or hire a daytime aide?

options.text: Hire a daytime aide from Brightside so Mom stays in her house

bases.narrative: Our furnace is 19 years old and needs a $2,000 repair to get through another winter. The alternative is replacing it with a heat pump; the installer's quote is $11,900 before the state rebate, and the rebate, which we would apply for after installation, takes $3,000 off. The installer estimates the heat pump would cut our heating bill by $60 a month, and it would take the house off gas entirely. My wife Ana and I are deciding this together, and nobody else has a say. We'll install the heat pump if and only if its price minus the state rebate comes to less than $8,000 more than the furnace repair; otherwise we'll repair the furnace. Nothing else is part of this decision for us.
bases.question: Should we replace the furnace with a heat pump or repair it?

bases.narrative: I'm deciding whether to put solar panels on my house. The installer quoted $20,000, the federal tax credit covers 30% of that, and the installer estimates the panels would save me $1,300 a year on electricity. They would cut my grid use by about 60%, and the installer's workmanship warranty is 10 years. I expect to stay in this house another 12 years. My partner has said this one is my call alone. I'll install solar if and only if the price after the tax credit, divided by the yearly savings, comes to fewer years than I expect to stay; otherwise I'll skip it. Nothing else is part of this decision for me.
bases.question: Should I install the solar panels or skip them?

bases.narrative: I start a new job in March and I'm choosing how to get there for the next two years.
